story: In George Orwell's novel Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949), Big Brother is the all-seeing leader of a totalitarian state, and posters everywhere warn citizens that “Big Brother is watching you.”
def: a powerful authority, usually a government or company, that watches and controls people's lives too closely
ex: With cameras tracking every keystroke, the new office software felt like Big Brother to the staff.
Privacy groups warned that the city's facial-recognition plan could turn into a Big Brother system.

cloze.s: Kwame covered his laptop camera, joking that he didn't want ___ watching him while he worked.

note: The reality TV show of the same name borrowed it from the novel.

story: In Joseph Heller's 1961 novel Catch-22, a bomber pilot can be excused from deadly missions if he is insane, but asking to be excused proves he is sane, so no one escapes.
def: a no-win situation in which the rules or conditions contradict each other, leaving no way out
ex: It's a Catch-22: you need job experience to get hired, but you need to be hired to gain experience.
Maria faced a Catch-22 because the bank wanted a credit history before giving her the card that would build one.

cloze.s: The landlord demanded proof of income, but Diego couldn't start his job without an address—a classic ___.

story: Ebenezer Scrooge is the bitter old miser in Charles Dickens's A Christmas Carol (1843), who hoards his money and scorns Christmas until three spirits visit him.
def: a stingy, mean-spirited person who hates spending money or sharing with others
ex: Don't be such a Scrooge—chip in five dollars for Hannah's birthday cake.
Critics called the company a Scrooge after it canceled holiday bonuses despite record profits.

cloze.s: Uncle Tomás complained about every penny spent on gifts, earning the family nickname ___.

story: In Robert Louis Stevenson's 1886 novella Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde, a respected doctor drinks a potion that turns him into the cruel, violent Mr. Hyde.
def: a person with two sharply opposed sides to their character, one pleasant and one nasty
ex: Our coach is a real Jekyll and Hyde: friendly at practice, furious on game day.
Wei's Jekyll and Hyde personality behind the wheel shocked his calm, polite coworkers.

cloze.s: She was charming with clients but cruel to her assistants, a ___ act that eventually got her fired.

story: In Mary Shelley's 1818 novel Frankenstein, the scientist Victor Frankenstein builds and brings to life a creature that he then abandons, and it turns against him.
def: a creation that escapes its maker's control and ends up causing harm
ex: The tax code has become a Frankenstein's monster of patches, loopholes, and exceptions.
Aisha's quick weekend app grew into a Frankenstein's monster nobody on her team could maintain.

cloze.s: The startup's chatbot, stitched together from five old programs, became a ___ that insulted customers.

note: In the novel, Frankenstein is the scientist, not the creature, though many people use the name for both.

story: Peter Pan, created by J. M. Barrie in a 1904 play and later a novel, is a boy who lives in Neverland and refuses ever to grow up.
def: an adult who avoids maturing and the responsibilities that come with adulthood
ex: At forty, Liam still lives like a Peter Pan, skipping bills and sleeping until noon.
The magazine profiled Peter Pan types who avoid commitment and chase endless fun.

cloze.s: My brother refuses to get a steady job or sign a lease, playing ___ well into his thirties.

story: In Dr. Seuss's 1957 book How the Grinch Stole Christmas!, a grumpy green creature tries to ruin the holiday by stealing a town's presents and decorations.
def: a grouchy spoilsport who tries to ruin other people's fun, especially during holidays
ex: The neighbor who complained about our holiday lights was a total Grinch.
Don't be a Grinch—let the kids stay up late for the New Year's countdown.

cloze.s: Malik played the ___ when he canceled the office holiday party to save a few hundred dollars.

story: Sherlock Holmes is the brilliant detective created by Arthur Conan Doyle, first appearing in A Study in Scarlet (1887), famous for solving crimes through sharp observation and logic.
def: a sharp-eyed person who cleverly figures things out from small clues; often used sarcastically
ex: Priya worked out who ate her lunch from the crumbs alone—a real Sherlock Holmes.
“The store is closed because the lights are off? Thanks, Sherlock Holmes,” Jamal said with a grin.

cloze.s: Spotting the tiny typo that broke the whole website, Yuki earned the nickname ___ from her team.

note: The sarcastic “No kidding, Sherlock” mocks someone for stating the obvious.

story: Romeo is the young lover in Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet who falls passionately for Juliet, the daughter of his family's enemies.
def: a man who ardently woos women; a passionate male lover or would-be lover
ex: Diego turned into a real Romeo, leaving flowers and poems on Sofia's desk all week.
The movie's hero is a smooth-talking Romeo who charms everyone at the wedding.

cloze.s: Grandpa still plays the ___, bringing Grandma roses and singing to her every anniversary.

note: In Juliet's line “wherefore art thou Romeo?” the word wherefore means “why,” not “where.”

story: In Shakespeare's The Merry Wives of Windsor, Pistol declares, “Why, then the world's mine oyster, / Which I with sword will open,” meaning he will seize his fortune by force.
def: you have the freedom and opportunity to do anything or go anywhere you want
ex: Fresh out of college with no debt, Fatima felt the world was her oyster.
Speak three languages, and the world is your oyster when it comes to travel jobs.

cloze.s: Now that the kids are grown and you've retired, ___—go travel wherever you like.

term: to be or not to be
story: “To be, or not to be, that is the question” opens Hamlet's most famous soliloquy, in which the grieving prince debates whether to keep enduring life's suffering or end it.
def: a phrase used, often playfully, to frame a basic decision about whether to do something at all
ex: To be or not to be a homeowner—that's the question Olga keeps debating as her rent rises.
For the band, the choice was to be or not to be: tour again or finally split up.

cloze.s: Staring at the gym membership form, Liam muttered, “___—that is the question.”
cloze.a: To be or not to be

note: In the play the speech is deeply serious; jokey modern uses usually drop that weight.

story: The saying is named after Edward A. Murphy Jr., an American aerospace engineer who worked on Air Force rocket-sled tests around 1949; the exact original wording and story are disputed.
def: the joking rule that anything that can possibly go wrong eventually will
ex: Murphy's law struck again: the printer jammed five minutes before Kwame's big presentation.
Pack an umbrella—by Murphy's law, it'll rain the moment you leave it home.

cloze.s: The car broke down, the phone died, and the hotel lost our booking—___ in full effect.

story: Harry Houdini (1874–1926), a Hungarian-born American performer, became world famous for escaping from handcuffs, straitjackets, chains, and locked tanks of water.
def: a person remarkably skilled at escaping from tight spots or vanishing unnoticed
ex: Our cat is a Houdini—she slipped out of a zipped carrier at the vet.
Jamal pulled a Houdini and disappeared right before it was time to wash the dishes.

cloze.s: The toddler is a little ___, climbing out of his crib and over the baby gate every night.

story: Albert Einstein (1879–1955) was the German-born physicist behind the theory of relativity, and his name became a byword for genius.
def: a very intelligent person, a genius; often used sarcastically for someone who is not
ex: You don't have to be an Einstein to see that the budget doesn't add up.
Our new intern is a real Einstein with spreadsheets—she automated the whole report.

cloze.s: “Nice job locking the keys in the running car, ___,” Sofia teased her brother.

story: Austrian neurologist Sigmund Freud argued in The Psychopathology of Everyday Life (1901) that slips of the tongue can reveal hidden, unconscious thoughts or wishes.
def: an accidental verbal mistake thought to reveal what the speaker is really thinking or feeling
ex: The host called the speech “long-awaited—I mean long-winded,” a Freudian slip that got big laughs.
When Wei called his new girlfriend by his ex's name, he insisted it wasn't a Freudian slip.

cloze.s: The manager said she was “thrilled to fire—er, hire—” the new team, a ___ everyone noticed.

story: A placebo is a dummy treatment, such as a sugar pill; the word is Latin for “I shall please.” In medical trials, patients given placebos often improve simply because they expect to.
def: an improvement in someone's condition caused by their belief in a treatment rather than the treatment itself
ex: The new supplement worked no better than sugar pills, suggesting its benefits were the placebo effect.
Hannah thinks her lucky socks help her run faster, but it's probably the placebo effect.

cloze.s: Patients who took the fake pill still felt less pain, showing a strong ___.

note: Its opposite is the nocebo effect, where expecting harm makes people feel worse.

story: On June 18, 1815, Napoleon Bonaparte suffered his final defeat near Waterloo, in present-day Belgium, against British-led allied and Prussian armies, ending his rule.
def: a final, decisive defeat, especially for someone who had long been successful
ex: The undefeated chess champion finally met her Waterloo against a twelve-year-old prodigy.
Rising interest rates proved to be the Waterloo of the once-booming real estate firm.

cloze.s: After ten straight wins, the team met its ___ in the championship, losing by thirty points.

note: Usually in the phrase “meet one's Waterloo.”

story: After gold was found at Sutter's Mill in California in January 1848, hundreds of thousands of fortune seekers poured into the region, many arriving in 1849.
def: a sudden stampede of people hurrying to cash in on a new, profitable opportunity
ex: The rise of electric cars set off a gold rush for lithium mining rights.
When the app went viral, there was a gold rush of copycats trying to match it.

cloze.s: Investors flooded into tiny AI startups in a frantic ___, hoping to strike it rich.

story: The American frontier of the late 1800s is remembered, partly through dime novels and Hollywood Westerns, as a rough region of cowboys, outlaws, and little law enforcement.
def: a situation or field with few rules or controls, where anything goes and disorder reigns
ex: Early internet advertising was the Wild West, with almost no privacy rules.
Investors called the crypto market the Wild West after a string of collapses.

cloze.s: Before regulators stepped in, the scooter-rental business was ___, with bikes dumped on every sidewalk.

story: In military planning, “D-Day” marks the day an operation begins; the most famous is June 6, 1944, when Allied forces landed on the beaches of Normandy, France, in World War II.
def: the date on which an important, long-planned operation or event is set to begin
ex: Moving D-Day is Saturday, so Aisha booked the truck and bought boxes.
The product team counted down the weeks until launch D-Day.

cloze.s: After months of planning, Friday is ___ for the hospital's new computer system to go live.

story: In 1970, after an oxygen tank exploded aboard Apollo 13, astronaut Jack Swigert radioed, “Houston, we've had a problem,” and Jim Lovell repeated it. The 1995 film Apollo 13 changed the line to “we have a problem.”
def: a humorous way to announce that something has suddenly gone seriously wrong
ex: Houston, we have a problem: the caterer just canceled an hour before the wedding.
Tomás opened the spreadsheet, saw the totals, and said, “Houston, we have a problem.”

cloze.s: Looking at the flooded basement, Yuki called upstairs, “___—bring towels!”

story: The Roman writer Vitruvius reported that the Greek scientist Archimedes, seeing his bathwater rise, suddenly understood how to measure an object's volume and ran out shouting “Eureka!”, Greek for “I have found it!”
def: a sudden flash of insight when the answer to a problem becomes clear
ex: Priya had her eureka moment in the shower: the bug was a missing decimal point.
The coach's eureka moment came when he moved his fastest player to defense.

cloze.s: After weeks of failed experiments, Dr. Okafor had a ___ while walking her dog.

note: Vitruvius wrote about two centuries after Archimedes, so the bathtub scene may be legend.

story: In Patrick Hamilton's 1938 play Gas Light and the 1944 film Gaslight, a husband secretly dims the house's gas lamps and insists his wife is imagining it, trying to make her doubt her sanity.
def: manipulating someone into doubting their own memory, perceptions, or sanity
ex: He kept denying he had said things she remembered clearly—classic gaslighting.
Therapists say gaslighting can happen at work when a boss insists your accurate notes are wrong.

cloze.s: Telling Olga she imagined the argument, even though three people heard it, was ___.

story: In the 1993 film Groundhog Day, a cynical TV weatherman played by Bill Murray finds himself living the same February 2 in Punxsutawney, Pennsylvania, over and over.
def: a situation in which the same tedious events seem to repeat endlessly
ex: Working from home during the long winter felt like Groundhog Day for Malik.
Every budget meeting is Groundhog Day: same complaints, same charts, no decisions.

cloze.s: Same commute, same lunch, same arguments—Fatima felt she was stuck in ___.

story: The Twilight Zone, Rod Serling's TV series that began in 1959, told eerie, surreal stories in which ordinary people slipped into strange realities, often with twist endings.
def: a bizarre, unsettling situation that feels unreal, as though normal rules no longer apply
ex: Walking into his childhood home, now a coffee shop, felt like entering the Twilight Zone.
When everyone at the meeting agreed with the intern's wild plan, Hannah felt she was in the Twilight Zone.

cloze.s: My boss praising my late report and giving me Friday off? I must be in ___.

story: In Superman comics, radio shows, and films, kryptonite is a glowing mineral from his destroyed home planet, Krypton, and the one substance that can weaken him.
def: the one specific weakness that can bring down an otherwise strong person
ex: Chocolate cake is my kryptonite; I can't say no to a slice.
Left-handed pitchers have been the slugger's kryptonite all season.

cloze.s: Diego can resist any sale except bookstore discounts—they're his ___.

story: Martin Handford's picture books, first published in Britain in 1987 as Where's Wally?, challenge readers to find a man in a red-and-white striped shirt hidden in huge crowded scenes; North American editions call him Waldo.
def: a hard search for one person or thing hidden in a busy crowd or cluttered scene
ex: Finding Jamal in the packed stadium was a game of Where's Waldo.
The error buried in the 200-page contract was a real Where's Waldo for the legal team.

cloze.s: Spotting my red suitcase among hundreds on the airport carousel felt like playing ___.

story: George Orwell, the pen name of Eric Blair, wrote Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949) and Animal Farm (1945), portraying regimes that spy on citizens, rewrite history, and twist language to control thought.
def: describing heavy-handed surveillance, propaganda, or control that twists the truth and limits freedom
ex: Critics called the plan to monitor employees' personal social media accounts downright Orwellian.
Renaming layoffs “talent liberation” struck the staff as Orwellian doublespeak.

cloze.s: The school's plan to track students' every keystroke at home sounded ___ to worried parents.

story: Niccolò Machiavelli (1469–1527), a Florentine diplomat, wrote The Prince, advising rulers that deceit and ruthlessness can be justified to win and keep power.
def: cunning, scheming, and willing to deceive or manipulate others to get ahead
ex: The Machiavellian manager took credit for his team's ideas to win a promotion.
In the drama, the queen's Machiavellian adviser plays every faction against the others.

cloze.s: Spreading rumors to sink her rival's campaign for club president was a ___ move that worked—for a while.

story: In Eleanor H. Porter's 1913 novel Pollyanna, an orphaned girl plays “the glad game,” always finding something to be glad about no matter what happens.
def: a person who is cheerfully optimistic to the point of ignoring real problems
ex: Don't be a Pollyanna about the merger—some jobs will definitely be cut.
Kwame's Pollyanna attitude kept the team upbeat, but it also hid the deadline risks.

cloze.s: Even after the flood ruined her basement, the ___ next door called it a great chance to redecorate.

note: Usually mildly critical: it suggests naive, unrealistic cheerfulness.

story: Thomas More's 1516 book Utopia describes an imaginary island with an ideal society; he built the name from Greek words meaning “no place,” a pun on a similar Greek word for “good place.”
def: an imagined perfect place or society where everyone lives in harmony and happiness
ex: The founders promised a tech utopia, but the town ended up with traffic jams and high rents.
For Sofia, a quiet library with endless coffee is pure utopia.

cloze.s: No society is perfect; anyone selling you a ___ is ignoring human nature.

story: In Lewis Carroll's Alice's Adventures in Wonderland (1865), Alice follows a White Rabbit down a rabbit hole and tumbles into a bizarre, illogical world.
def: getting pulled deeper and deeper into a strange, absorbing, or time-consuming topic or situation
ex: Liam went down the rabbit hole of family history and spent all night on genealogy sites.
One video about sourdough sent Hannah down the rabbit hole for weeks.

cloze.s: I looked up one fact about octopuses and went ___, reading until three in the morning.

story: In J. K. Rowling's Harry Potter books, first published in 1997, “Muggles” are ordinary people with no magical powers.
def: an outsider who lacks the special skill or knowledge of a particular group
ex: To us coding muggles, the engineers' jargon sounded like a foreign language.
The guide explains wine tasting for muggles who just want something nice with dinner.

cloze.s: At the chess club, Aisha felt like a ___ while everyone else debated opening theory.

story: The prologue to Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet calls the pair “star-crossed lovers,” meaning thwarted by the stars, or fate, since their feuding families doom their romance.
def: a couple whose romance is doomed by bad luck or forces beyond their control
ex: The novel follows star-crossed lovers separated by war and closed borders.
Grandma says she and Grandpa were star-crossed lovers until her parents finally gave in.

cloze.s: Divided by rival families and a court order, the two teens were ___ from the start.

story: The phrase first appears in print in Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet, where Mercutio uses it for a horseback game in which riders had to follow a leader's unpredictable course.
def: a long, hopeless search for something that cannot be found or does not exist
ex: The vague directions sent us on a wild-goose chase around the neighborhood.
Searching every store for last year's model turned into a wild-goose chase for Malik.

cloze.s: The tip about treasure hidden in the attic was a hoax that sent us on a ___.

story: In Hamlet, the courtier Polonius, puzzled by the prince's odd behavior, remarks, “Though this be madness, yet there is method in't.”
def: a sensible purpose or plan hidden behind behavior that looks strange or chaotic
ex: Her desk looks like a disaster, but there's method in the madness—she can find anything in seconds.
The coach's odd lineup had method in the madness: it confused the other team completely.

cloze.s: The chef's chaotic-looking kitchen has ___: every tool sits exactly where she reaches for it.

note: Also heard as “method to the madness.”

story: The Watergate scandal began with a 1972 break-in at the Democratic National Committee offices in Washington's Watergate complex; the cover-up led to President Richard Nixon's resignation in 1974.
def: a suffix added to a word to name a scandal, especially one involving a cover-up
ex: Reporters love tacking “-gate” onto any scandal, from sports cheating to celebrity feuds.
When someone kept stealing lunches from the office fridge, coworkers dubbed the mystery “Yogurt-gate.”

cloze.s: The paper attached the suffix ___ to the mayor's parking-ticket scandal, making it sound even bigger.

story: Ancient Sparta, a Greek city-state, was famous for the strict military training of its citizens and their simple, tough, comfort-free way of life.
def: very plain and simple, with no comforts or luxuries; also strictly disciplined
ex: The dorm room was Spartan: a bed, a desk, and one bare lightbulb.
Olga follows a Spartan training routine, running at 5 a.m. even in the snow.

cloze.s: The hostel was ___ but clean, with bare walls, thin mattresses, and no Wi-Fi.

note: Often written lowercase (spartan).

story: In 1961, President John F. Kennedy set the goal of landing an American on the moon before the decade ended; the Apollo program achieved it in July 1969.
def: an extremely ambitious, risky project aimed at a breakthrough that seems almost impossible
ex: The company's cancer-vaccine program is a moonshot that may take decades to pay off.
Building a carbon-free city in ten years is a moonshot, but the planners are committed.

cloze.s: Curing the disease outright was a ___, so the lab also funded smaller, safer studies.

story: Ground zero was the military term for the point directly beneath a nuclear explosion, used for the 1945 atomic bomb sites; after September 11, 2001, it also named the site of New York's World Trade Center.
def: the central point where something starts or where its effects are strongest
ex: The small lab in Boston became ground zero for the new gene-editing industry.
Our kitchen was ground zero for the flood after the dishwasher hose burst.

cloze.s: Doctors traced the outbreak back to a single restaurant, which was ___ for the illness.

story: Coal miners once carried caged canaries underground because the birds react to toxic gases such as carbon monoxide before people do; a sick canary warned miners to get out. British mines used them until 1986.
def: an early warning sign of approaching danger or trouble
ex: Falling sales at small shops can be a canary in a coal mine for the wider economy.
Doctors see rising childhood asthma as a canary in a coal mine for air pollution.

cloze.s: Dying frogs in the pond were the ___, warning that the town's water was contaminated.

story: During a 1973 bank robbery in Stockholm, Sweden, hostages held for six days came to sympathize with their captors and later defended them; the term was coined afterward.
def: a bond or sympathy that captives or victims develop toward the people controlling or mistreating them
ex: Employees defending the boss who underpaid them joked that they had Stockholm syndrome.
Experts note that Stockholm syndrome is not an official psychiatric diagnosis.

cloze.s: After years with the abusive coach, the players still praised him, which their parents feared was ___.

note: Not an official diagnosis; researchers debate how real or common it is.

story: In physics, a quantum leap or jump is an electron's sudden switch between energy levels inside an atom, an extremely tiny change. Everyday use flipped the meaning to a huge advance.
def: a sudden, dramatic advance or improvement
ex: The smartphone was a quantum leap over the clunky cell phones of the 1990s.
Hiring a full-time coach brought a quantum leap in the team's performance.

cloze.s: Switching from paper charts to digital records was a ___ in how quickly the clinic could see patients.

note: Ironically, a real quantum jump in physics is incredibly small.

story: English philosopher Herbert Spencer coined the phrase in 1864 after reading Charles Darwin; Darwin adopted it in later editions of On the Origin of Species as another name for natural selection.
def: the idea that those best adapted to their surroundings or competition are the ones that thrive
ex: In the cutthroat restaurant business, it's survival of the fittest.
The reality show was pure survival of the fittest, with one contestant cut each week.

cloze.s: Only the best-run bookstores lasted after online shopping took off—a case of ___.

note: In biology, fittest means best suited to the environment, not strongest.

story: Giacomo Casanova (1725–1798) was a Venetian adventurer and writer whose memoir describes his many love affairs across Europe.
def: a man known for seducing or romancing many women
ex: Tomás fancies himself a Casanova, but his pickup lines usually fall flat.
The sitcom's neighbor is a Casanova who shows up with a new date every episode.

cloze.s: Hannah warned her friend that the charming bartender was a ___ who flirted with every customer.

story: Samuel Maverick (1803–1870), a Texas lawyer and landowner, did not brand his cattle, so unbranded strays came to be called “mavericks.”
def: an independent-minded person who refuses to follow the group or the usual rules
ex: The maverick chef ignored tradition and served tacos at the formal gala.
As a maverick in the lab, Yuki tested ideas her colleagues had dismissed.

cloze.s: Always ignoring the playbook and trying risky moves, the quarterback had a reputation as a ___.

story: In 1920, Charles Ponzi promised Boston investors 50 percent returns in 45 days, supposedly from trading international postal coupons, but paid early investors with money from new ones until it collapsed.
def: a fraud in which earlier investors are paid with money from newer investors instead of real profits
ex: The investment club turned out to be a Ponzi scheme that wiped out retirees' savings.
Regulators warned that the fund's guaranteed high returns looked like a Ponzi scheme.

cloze.s: The “guaranteed 20 percent monthly profits” were really a ___ that collapsed when new money stopped coming in.

note: Similar to a pyramid scheme, in which members profit mainly by recruiting others.

story: It is named after Napoleon Bonaparte, popularly imagined as tiny; he was in fact about 5 feet 6 or 7 inches, roughly average for his time, and British cartoons helped spread the myth.
def: aggressive or domineering behavior believed to make up for a person's short height
ex: Malik joked that his small dog had a Napoleon complex, barking at every Great Dane.
The article questioned whether the Napoleon complex is real or just a stereotype.

cloze.s: The short, bossy supervisor shouted at everyone, and staff whispered that he had a ___.

note: A pop-psychology term; studies give mixed evidence that it exists.

story: Debbie Downer is a recurring Saturday Night Live character, played by Rachel Dratch beginning in 2004, who spoils every happy moment with gloomy news.
def: a person who constantly brings up depressing news and dampens everyone's mood
ex: I hate to be a Debbie Downer, but the forecast says rain all weekend.
Every time we plan a trip, Liam plays Debbie Downer and lists everything that could go wrong.

cloze.s: At the party, Jamal kept talking about layoffs and illness, becoming the group's ___.

story: In the 1996 film Jerry Maguire, football player Rod Tidwell (Cuba Gooding Jr.) makes his sports agent (Tom Cruise) shout “Show me the money!” over the phone.
def: a demand to see real payment or financial proof rather than promises
ex: The athlete liked the team's pitch, but his agent said, “Show me the money.”
“Nice business plan—now show me the money,” the investor told the young founders.

cloze.s: Tired of vague promises of a raise, Aisha finally told her boss, “___.”

story: In the 1939 film The Wizard of Oz, after a tornado carries Dorothy from Kansas to the magical Land of Oz, she tells her dog, “Toto, I've a feeling we're not in Kansas anymore.”
def: a remark that one is suddenly in a strange, unfamiliar place or situation
ex: Stepping into Tokyo's busy Shibuya crossing, Diego laughed, “We're not in Kansas anymore.”
The new job had dress codes and badge scanners everywhere—clearly we're not in Kansas anymore.

cloze.s: Seeing camels on the road outside the airport, Sofia whispered to her sister, “___.”

story: In Mario Puzo's 1969 novel The Godfather and the 1972 film, Mafia boss Vito Corleone says he will make a reluctant man “an offer he can't refuse,” a threat dressed up as a deal.
def: a proposal so attractive, or so threatening, that saying no is not realistically possible
ex: Double the salary and a corner office? That's an offer you can't refuse.
The landlord made the tenants an offer they couldn't refuse: leave now or face a costly lawsuit.

cloze.s: Free tuition plus a guaranteed job afterward was ___, so Kwame signed immediately.

story: The phrase comes from Keeping Up with the Joneses, a comic strip by Arthur R. “Pop” Momand that began in 1913, about a family straining to match their neighbors' lifestyle.
def: trying to match the possessions and lifestyle of neighbors or peers to avoid seeming inferior
ex: They bought a second car they couldn't afford just to keep up with the Joneses.
Keeping up with the Joneses on social media can leave people anxious and in debt.

cloze.s: After the neighbors installed a pool, Dad wanted one too—a classic case of ___.

story: The line “In the future, everybody will be world-famous for 15 minutes” appeared in a 1968 exhibition catalog for artist Andy Warhol and is credited to him, though its exact authorship has been questioned.
def: a brief, fleeting burst of public attention, usually for something minor
ex: After his dancing video went viral, Wei enjoyed fifteen minutes of fame on morning TV.
Most reality-show contestants get their fifteen minutes of fame and then vanish.

cloze.s: The woman who grew the giant pumpkin had her ___, appearing on the local news for one night.

story: Franz Kafka (1883–1924), a Prague-born writer, depicted nightmarish bureaucracies; in The Trial, Josef K. is arrested and prosecuted by a remote authority without ever learning his crime.
def: nightmarishly confusing, illogical, and oppressive, especially in dealings with a faceless bureaucracy
ex: Getting a refund required a Kafkaesque maze of forms, hold music, and dead-end emails.
The paperwork turned Fatima's simple visa renewal into a Kafkaesque ordeal.

cloze.s: Each office told Liam he needed a form that only the other office could issue—a truly ___ situation.

story: In Miguel de Cervantes's Don Quixote (1605 and 1615), a Spanish gentleman obsessed with tales of chivalry sets out as a knight to right the world's wrongs, with absurd results.
def: idealistic and noble-minded but wildly impractical or unrealistic
ex: Her quixotic plan to abolish homework across the district never got past the first meeting.
Running for city council with no money was quixotic, but Jamal wanted to raise the issue.

cloze.s: Trying to stop the giant chain store with a one-person protest was a brave but ___ effort.

note: Pronounced kwik-SOT-ik in English.

story: In James Hilton's 1933 novel Lost Horizon, Shangri-La is a hidden valley in the mountains of Tibet where people live in peace and age remarkably slowly.
def: an idyllic, remote paradise, far from the troubles of the ordinary world
ex: The tiny island resort was a Shangri-La with no cars, no phones, and endless beaches.
For Olga, the cabin by the lake is her personal Shangri-La.

cloze.s: After years in the noisy city, the couple found their ___ in a peaceful mountain village.

story: In 49 BC, Julius Caesar led his army across the Rubicon, a small river in northern Italy, breaking Roman law against generals bringing troops into Italy and starting a civil war.
def: taking an irreversible step that commits one to a course of action
ex: Signing the restaurant lease was Priya's crossing the Rubicon—no going back to her office job.
Once the company announced the merger publicly, it had crossed the Rubicon.

cloze.s: Selling the house and moving abroad was ___ for the family; there was no way back.

story: King Pyrrhus of Epirus defeated Roman armies in 280 and 279 BC but lost so many soldiers that, according to Plutarch, he said another such win would ruin him.
def: a win that costs the winner so much that it is hardly worth it
ex: Winning the lawsuit was a Pyrrhic victory; the legal fees bankrupted the company.
The team won the game but lost its star player to injury—a Pyrrhic victory.

cloze.s: Hannah got her way in the family argument, but no one spoke to her for months—a real ___.

story: In Shakespeare's Julius Caesar (1599), Caesar gasps “Et tu, Brute?” (“You too, Brutus?”) when his friend joins the assassins. No ancient source records the real Caesar saying these words.
def: an expression of shocked hurt at being betrayed by a trusted friend or ally
ex: When her best friend voted for the other plan, Sofia muttered, “Et tu, Brute?”
The coach had an “Et tu, Brute?” moment when his longtime assistant joined the rival team.

cloze.s: Even my own sister took Dad's side in the argument? ___

note: Suetonius reports, as a rumor, that Caesar said “You too, child?” in Greek.

story: In Shakespeare's Othello, the scheming Iago warns Othello, “O, beware, my lord, of jealousy; / It is the green-eyed monster which doth mock / The meat it feeds on.”
def: jealousy, pictured as a creature that torments the person who feels it
ex: The green-eyed monster appeared when Diego saw his ex laughing with someone new.
Social media can awaken the green-eyed monster as friends post vacation photos.

cloze.s: When her coworker got the promotion she wanted, Maria struggled to tame the ___.

story: In Shakespeare's As You Like It, the melancholy Jaques begins his “seven ages of man” speech with “All the world's a stage, / And all the men and women merely players.”
def: the idea that life is like a play in which everyone performs roles
ex: All the world's a stage, Kwame reminded himself as he smiled through the awkward interview.
Influencers posing for every meal seem to prove that all the world's a stage.

cloze.s: Watching shoppers act cheerful for the cameras, the novelist thought, “___, and we are all actors.”

story: In Shakespeare's The Merchant of Venice, the moneylender Shylock lends money to Antonio on the condition that if it is not repaid, he may cut away a pound of Antonio's flesh.
def: a harsh repayment or penalty demanded in full, even though it causes great harm
ex: The lender wanted its pound of flesh, piling on fees until the family lost their home.
Angry fans demanded their pound of flesh after the embarrassing loss, calling for the coach's firing.

cloze.s: Even after Malik apologized and repaid the loan, his cousin still wanted his ___ in interest and humiliation.

term: the lady doth protest too much
story: In Hamlet, Queen Gertrude watches a play in which a queen vows never to remarry and remarks, “The lady doth protest too much, methinks.” In Shakespeare's day, protest meant to vow or declare.
def: said when someone's overly insistent denial makes it seem likely the opposite is true
ex: Liam swore ten times he wasn't jealous—the lady doth protest too much.
The company's endless statements insisting nothing was wrong made analysts think the lady doth protest too much.

cloze.s: Every time someone mentions his ex, Tomás loudly insists he's totally over her; ___, I think.
cloze.a: the lady doth protest too much

note: Often misquoted as “Methinks the lady doth protest too much.”

term: brevity is the soul of wit
story: In Hamlet, the long-winded courtier Polonius declares that “brevity is the soul of wit” and then keeps rambling, which is part of the joke.
def: the idea that saying things concisely is the key to clever, effective communication
ex: Remember that brevity is the soul of wit, and keep your wedding toast under two minutes.
The editor cut the article in half, reminding Yuki that brevity is the soul of wit.

cloze.s: The best jokes are short and sharp; as the saying goes, ___.
cloze.a: brevity is the soul of wit

story: In Macbeth, as Macbeth weighs murdering King Duncan, he wishes that the deed “might be the be-all and the end-all here,” settling everything with no consequences.
def: the single most important thing; the ultimate goal or deciding factor
ex: Test scores aren't the be-all and end-all of a good education.
For Aisha, winning the championship was the be-all and end-all of the season.

cloze.s: Money isn't the ___ of a career; meaning and good colleagues matter too.

story: The Ides of March, March 15 in the Roman calendar, was the day Julius Caesar was assassinated in 44 BC. In Shakespeare's Julius Caesar, a soothsayer warns him, “Beware the ides of March.”
def: a date that brings, or is feared to bring, betrayal or disaster
ex: With layoffs announced for mid-March, the staff grimly joked about the Ides of March.
“Beware the Ides of March,” Grandpa warned, reminding us that the tax deadline was close.

cloze.s: The vote that ousted the club's president fell on March 15, and members joked about the ___.

story: In German legend, the scholar Faust sells his soul to the devil, Mephistopheles, in exchange for knowledge and power; the tale was famously retold by Christopher Marlowe and by Johann Wolfgang von Goethe.
def: a deal in which someone gives up their values or long-term well-being for short-term power or success
ex: Taking the high-paying job at a company she distrusted felt like a Faustian bargain to Priya.
The band's Faustian bargain with the record label brought fame but cost them control of their music.

cloze.s: Trading his health and family time for a huge bonus was a ___ that Diego later regretted.

story: In Washington Irving's 1819 short story, Rip Van Winkle falls asleep in New York's Catskill Mountains for twenty years and wakes to find the American Revolution has come and gone.
def: a person badly out of touch with changes that happened while they were away or not paying attention
ex: After five years at a remote research station, Olga felt like Rip Van Winkle in a world of new apps.
The executive acted like Rip Van Winkle, unaware that his customers now shopped online.

cloze.s: Back from ten years at sea, the captain was a ___, amazed that everyone paid with their phones.

story: Benedict Arnold was an American general in the Revolutionary War who, in 1780, plotted to surrender the fort at West Point to the British and then fought on the British side.
def: a traitor, especially someone who betrays their own side or friends
ex: When the star player signed with their bitter rivals, angry fans called him a Benedict Arnold.
Hannah felt like a Benedict Arnold for switching to the competing coffee shop across the street.

cloze.s: Leaking the team's plans to the rival company made Jamal the office ___.

story: Between 1811 and 1816, English textile workers called Luddites smashed new machines they blamed for wrecking their wages and jobs; they took their name from “Ned Ludd,” a probably mythical leader.
def: a person who opposes or distrusts new technology
ex: Grandpa is a proud Luddite who still writes letters and refuses to own a smartphone.
Calling every critic of the new software a Luddite ignores their valid security concerns.

cloze.s: Sofia refuses to use online banking or GPS, cheerfully calling herself a ___.

note: The original Luddites opposed machines that threatened their livelihoods, not technology as such.

story: Russian scientist Ivan Pavlov showed around 1900 that dogs who repeatedly got a signal just before being fed would start salivating at the signal alone, a process now called classical conditioning.
def: describing an automatic, learned reaction to a signal, made without conscious thought
ex: Kwame has a Pavlovian reaction to the ice cream truck's jingle.
The whole office reacts with Pavlovian speed whenever someone says “free pizza.”

cloze.s: Every time her phone buzzes, Maria grabs it with ___ urgency, even during dinner.

note: The story is usually told with a bell, but his lab used various signals, including metronomes and buzzers.

story: Meteorologist Edward Lorenz found that tiny changes in a weather model's starting numbers produced wildly different forecasts; his 1972 talk asked whether a butterfly's wing flap in Brazil could set off a tornado in Texas.
def: the idea that a tiny change can set off a chain of events with huge consequences
ex: Missing one train set off a butterfly effect that led Wei to meet his future wife.
Economists warn of a butterfly effect in which one small bank failure spreads worldwide.

cloze.s: One typo in the code caused a ___ that eventually crashed the airline's entire booking system.

story: In 1880, tenants and neighbors in County Mayo, Ireland, refused to work for, trade with, or speak to Captain Charles Boycott, a land agent who tried to evict tenants; his name became the word for this tactic.
def: to refuse to buy from, use, or deal with a person, company, or country as a protest
ex: Students boycotted the cafeteria after it raised prices without warning.
Fans threatened to boycott the tournament over the sky-high ticket prices.

cloze.s: To protest the unsafe working conditions, customers agreed to ___ the factory's products until changes were made.

story: The idea goes back to Plato's dialogue the Symposium, which describes love rising from physical attraction toward a love of wisdom and beauty itself; Renaissance scholar Marsilio Ficino coined the phrase “Platonic love.”
def: close and affectionate but not romantic or sexual
ex: Malik and Sofia have a platonic friendship that has lasted since kindergarten.
Despite the rumors, the two co-stars insist their bond is strictly platonic.

cloze.s: They share an apartment and finish each other's sentences, but their relationship is purely ___.

story: Mickey Mouse, Walt Disney's cartoon character, became famous with the 1928 short Steamboat Willie. His name later came to mean small-time or childish, though exactly why is uncertain.
def: amateurish, trivial, or poorly run; not to be taken seriously
ex: The repair shop was a Mickey Mouse operation that lost Aisha's car keys twice.
Liam complained that the class was a Mickey Mouse course with no real assignments.

cloze.s: With no contracts and a website built in an afternoon, the agency looked like a ___ outfit.

story: In a 1977 episode of the sitcom Happy Days, the character Fonzie jumps over a shark on water skis; Jon Hein popularized the moment in the late 1990s as the sign of a long-running show turning to desperate gimmicks.
def: to pass one's peak and start declining, often by resorting to desperate gimmicks
ex: Fans say the series jumped the shark when the family moved to outer space.
The burger chain jumped the shark with its cereal-flavored milkshake burger.

cloze.s: Once the band released a holiday polka album, critics agreed it had ___.

story: Rube Goldberg (1883–1970) was an American cartoonist famous for drawings of absurdly complicated contraptions, chains of pulleys, balls, and animals, built to perform a simple task like wiping a diner's mouth.
def: an absurdly complicated contraption or process for accomplishing something simple
ex: Getting reimbursed for lunch required a Rube Goldberg machine of forms and approvals.
For the science fair, Yuki built a Rube Goldberg machine that cracks an egg in twenty steps.

cloze.s: The old billing system was a ___: nine programs passing data back and forth just to print one invoice.

story: Sherlock Holmes never says this exact line in Arthur Conan Doyle's stories, though he says “Elementary” and “my dear Watson” separately; the full phrase was popularized by later writers and films.
def: a smug remark that the answer is obvious and easy to work out
ex: “Elementary, my dear Watson,” Priya said, pointing at the muddy paw prints leading to the dog.
Asked how he knew it would rain, Grandpa said, “Elementary, my dear Watson—my knee aches.”

cloze.s: Asked how she found the missing remote, Sofia smirked, “___—it was under the cat.”

story: The line is popularly pinned on French queen Marie Antoinette, but there is no evidence she said it. Jean-Jacques Rousseau's Confessions, written when she was still a child in Austria, credits a similar remark to “a great princess.”
def: a phrase mocking a privileged person's clueless indifference to ordinary people's hardships
ex: When the CEO told struggling staff to “just invest more,” critics called it a let them eat cake moment.
Telling renters to simply buy houses instead struck many readers as a modern let them eat cake.

cloze.s: Told that the villagers had no bread, the spoiled duke in the play shrugs and says, “___.”

note: Rousseau's actual word was brioche, a rich bread, not cake.

story: On December 1, 1955, in Montgomery, Alabama, Rosa Parks was arrested for refusing to give up her bus seat to a white passenger; her protest sparked the Montgomery bus boycott, a landmark of the civil rights movement.
def: a single act of quiet, courageous defiance against injustice that inspires a broader movement
ex: The nurse's calm refusal to work unsafe double shifts became a Rosa Parks moment for the hospital staff.
Historians debate which protest was the true Rosa Parks moment for the farmworkers' campaign.

cloze.s: When the shy student calmly refused to follow the unfair rule, it became a ___ that changed the whole school.

note: Use with care: comparing small disputes to the civil rights movement can seem trivializing.

story: In Cervantes's Don Quixote, the deluded knight charges at a row of windmills with his lance, convinced they are giants; to tilt means to charge, as in a joust.
def: fighting imaginary enemies or pursuing hopeless battles against things that aren't real threats
ex: Fighting the city over a single parking ticket for three years felt like tilting at windmills.
Critics said the campaign was tilting at windmills, attacking problems that didn't exist.

cloze.s: Hannah spent months battling a rule that had already been repealed—she was ___.

story: According to the Roman historian Suetonius, Julius Caesar said “alea iacta est” (“the die is cast”) as he led his army across the Rubicon in 49 BC; Plutarch says he spoke it in Greek.
def: a decision has been made and events are now in motion, with no turning back
ex: The contracts are signed and the die is cast; the factory moves to Ohio next year.
Once Kwame hit send on his resignation email, the die was cast.

cloze.s: Malik has bought the one-way ticket and given up his apartment; ___.

note: Die here is the singular of dice.

term: something is rotten in the state of Denmark
story: In Hamlet, after the ghost of the murdered king appears, the guard Marcellus says, “Something is rotten in the state of Denmark,” sensing corruption at the heart of the royal court.
def: a sense that serious wrongdoing or corruption lurks within an organization or situation
ex: When auditors found missing invoices and shredded files, it was clear something is rotten in the state of Denmark.
Three managers quit in one week, and staff whispered that something is rotten in the state of Denmark.

cloze.s: The charity's director drove a sports car while its programs went unfunded—clearly ___.
cloze.a: something is rotten in the state of Denmark

story: In Shakespeare's Henry V, the king rallies his outnumbered troops before the Battle of Agincourt (1415) with the St. Crispin's Day speech: “We few, we happy few, we band of brothers.”
def: a close-knit group bound together by shared hardship or struggle
ex: After three years of night shifts together, the ER nurses became a band of brothers.
The underdog team played like a band of brothers, diving for every loose ball.

cloze.s: Surviving the startup's lean years together turned the founders into a true ___.

note: Also the title of a 1992 book and 2001 TV miniseries about World War II soldiers.

story: In Hamlet, after harshly confronting his mother about her marriage to his father's murderer, Hamlet says, “I must be cruel only to be kind.”
def: causing someone pain or upset now because it will help them in the long run
ex: Sometimes you have to be cruel to be kind and tell a friend their business idea won't work.
The physical therapist was cruel to be kind, pushing Fatima through painful rehab exercises.

cloze.s: Taking away the teenager's phone before exams was being ___, his mother insisted.

term: a rose by any other name
story: In Romeo and Juliet, Juliet argues that Romeo's family name doesn't matter: “What's in a name? That which we call a rose / By any other name would smell as sweet.”
def: the idea that what something really is matters more than what it is called
ex: Call it “rightsizing” if you like, but a rose by any other name—it's still a layoff.
A rose by any other name: the store-brand cereal tastes exactly like the famous one.

cloze.s: The cheaper generic medicine works just like the brand-name one; ___ would smell as sweet.
cloze.a: a rose by any other name

story: In William Golding's 1954 novel Lord of the Flies, a group of English schoolboys stranded on an island without adults slide from order into savagery and violence.
def: a situation in which people without rules or authority turn cruel and tribal
ex: With the teacher out sick and no substitute, the classroom turned into Lord of the Flies.
Without moderators, the online forum descended into a Lord of the Flies free-for-all.

cloze.s: When the power went out at summer camp, counselors had to stop a ___ scene in the cabins.

story: Charles Dickens (1812–1870) wrote novels such as Oliver Twist and Bleak House that exposed the grinding poverty, workhouses, and child labor of Victorian England.
def: reminiscent of grim poverty, squalor, and harsh working conditions, as in Victorian England
ex: The warehouse's Dickensian conditions—no heat, no breaks—sparked a state investigation.
Reporters described the crowded, rat-infested apartments as truly Dickensian.

cloze.s: Workers described ___ conditions: twelve-hour shifts, freezing rooms, and pay that barely covered food.

story: In James Thurber's 1939 short story “The Secret Life of Walter Mitty,” a meek, ordinary man escapes his dull life through vivid daydreams of being a hero.
def: an ordinary person who spends much time daydreaming about a far more exciting, heroic life
ex: Stuck in traffic, Diego became a Walter Mitty, imagining himself as a race-car champion.
The lawsuit revealed the executive was a Walter Mitty who had invented his military record.

cloze.s: Tomás, a quiet accountant, was a ___ who pictured himself as a jet pilot during every boring meeting.

story: In George du Maurier's 1894 novel Trilby, Svengali is a musician who hypnotizes a young woman, Trilby, and turns her into a star singer entirely under his control.
def: a person who exerts manipulative, controlling influence over someone else, often to shape their career
ex: The young singer's manager was called a Svengali who controlled every song and interview.
Critics described the coach as a Svengali, but the athletes credited him with their success.

cloze.s: Friends worried that her new business mentor had become a ___, dictating where she lived and whom she saw.

story: Akira Kurosawa's 1950 Japanese film Rashomon shows a deadly incident in a forest recounted by four witnesses, including a bandit and the dead man speaking through a medium, whose accounts contradict each other.
def: the way different people give conflicting yet believable accounts of the same event
ex: The car accident produced a Rashomon effect, with each driver blaming the other.
Historians face the Rashomon effect when eyewitness letters disagree about the same battle.

cloze.s: Every sibling remembered the family vacation completely differently—a classic ___.

story: Ancient writers reported rumors that Emperor Nero sang or performed while Rome burned in AD 64; the fiddle did not yet exist, and the historian Tacitus says Nero was away in Antium when the fire began.
def: to waste time on trivial matters, or do nothing, while a crisis grows worse
ex: While sales collapsed, the board fiddled while Rome burned, debating a new logo.
Critics accused the council of fiddling while Rome burns as the housing shortage deepened.

cloze.s: The manager kept reorganizing the break-room schedule as clients quit—he seemed content to ___.

story: Draco, a lawgiver in ancient Athens around 621 BC, wrote a legal code so harsh that, by tradition, even minor offenses were punished by death.
def: excessively harsh and severe, especially describing laws or punishments
ex: The school's draconian phone policy suspended students for sending a single text.
Critics called the bank's draconian late fees unfair to low-income customers.

cloze.s: A thousand-dollar fine for a library book returned one day late seemed ___ to Aisha.

term: rearranging deck chairs on the Titanic
story: The RMS Titanic sank on its first voyage in April 1912 after hitting an iceberg, killing more than 1,500 people; the phrase imagines crew uselessly tidying the deck as the ship went down.
def: making pointless, trivial changes while ignoring a much larger disaster
ex: Renaming departments while losing millions is just rearranging deck chairs on the Titanic.
To the overworked hospital staff, the new uniforms felt like rearranging deck chairs on the Titanic.

cloze.s: Cutting the office coffee budget when the company owes millions is like ___.
cloze.a: rearranging deck chairs on the Titanic

story: The Manhattan Project was the secret U.S.-led program, with British and Canadian participation, that developed the first atomic bombs during World War II.
def: a massive, urgent, heavily funded effort to solve one major problem quickly
ex: Scientists called for a Manhattan Project for clean energy to tackle climate change.
The hospital launched its own Manhattan Project to cut emergency-room wait times.

cloze.s: Experts urged a ___ for vaccine research, pooling thousands of scientists and billions of dollars.

story: Found by French soldiers in Egypt in 1799, the Rosetta Stone carries the same decree in Egyptian hieroglyphs, Demotic script, and ancient Greek, which helped Jean-François Champollion decipher hieroglyphs in 1822.
def: a key that unlocks understanding of something previously mysterious or hard to interpret
ex: The old lab notebook became the Rosetta Stone for understanding the inventor's designs.
For exhausted new parents, a good baby-sleep guide can feel like a Rosetta Stone.

cloze.s: The glossary at the back was the ___ that finally let Olga understand her insurance policy.

story: In a 1935 thought experiment, physicist Erwin Schrödinger imagined a cat sealed in a box whose life depends on a random atomic event, so quantum theory seemed to make it both alive and dead until observed, an absurdity he meant to highlight.
def: a situation whose outcome is uncertain, as if in two states at once, until someone checks
ex: Until I open the exam-results email, my grade is Schrödinger's cat: both pass and fail.
The leftover takeout in the fridge is Schrödinger's cat—fine or spoiled until you sniff it.

cloze.s: Until the doctor calls with the biopsy results, Kwame's diagnosis feels like ___.

story: In a 1999 study, Cornell psychologists David Dunning and Justin Kruger found that people who scored lowest on tests of skills such as logic and grammar tended to greatly overestimate how well they did.
def: the tendency of people with little skill or knowledge to overrate their own ability
ex: After one online course, Liam lectured doctors about vaccines—the Dunning-Kruger effect in action.
The Dunning-Kruger effect may explain why beginner chess players feel sure they can beat experts.

cloze.s: The rookie who had never managed anyone was certain he could run the company better than the CEO, a textbook ___.

note: Some researchers argue part of the pattern is a statistical artifact.

story: Swiss psychiatrist Hermann Rorschach published his inkblot test in 1921; people describe what they see in ambiguous blots, and their answers were thought to reveal their personality.
def: something ambiguous that people interpret in ways that reveal their own views or biases
ex: The abstract mural became a Rorschach test: some saw hope, others saw chaos.
The coach's vague statement was a Rorschach test, with each fan hearing what they wanted.

cloze.s: Readers saw the novel's ending as happy or tragic depending on their own mood; it was a literary ___.

story: Writer Fiona Broome coined the term around 2009 after finding that many people shared her false memory that Nelson Mandela had died in prison in the 1980s; he was freed in 1990 and died in 2013.
def: the phenomenon of many people sharing the same false memory of an event or detail
ex: Many people swear the Monopoly man wears a monocle, but he doesn't—a famous Mandela effect.
Hannah blamed the Mandela effect when her whole class misremembered the movie's famous line.

cloze.s: Millions remember the children's books as the “Berenstein Bears,” though the name was always “Berenstain”—the ___.

story: German physician Franz Anton Mesmer (1734–1815) claimed to cure patients with an invisible force he called “animal magnetism”; a 1784 French royal commission that included Benjamin Franklin found no evidence for it.
def: to hold someone's attention so completely that they seem to be in a trance
ex: The street performer's juggling mesmerized the crowd for twenty minutes.
Wei sat mesmerized by the northern lights dancing over the lake.

cloze.s: The toddler was so ___ by the aquarium's glowing jellyfish that she forgot about her snack.

story: In 2003, singer Barbra Streisand sued to suppress an aerial photo of her Malibu home that was part of a coastal-erosion archive; the lawsuit drew far more attention to the photo. Writer Mike Masnick coined the term in 2005.
def: the way an attempt to hide or censor information ends up spreading it more widely
ex: The company's demand to delete one bad review triggered the Streisand effect, and thousands shared it.
Banning the novel caused a Streisand effect that sent it to the top of the bestseller list.

cloze.s: The hotel's legal threat over a critical blog post backfired through the ___, making the post go viral.

story: The Art of War is an ancient Chinese treatise on military strategy traditionally credited to the general Sun Tzu (Sunzi) and written more than 2,000 years ago; its advice on deception and knowing your enemy is widely quoted today.
def: the classic ancient Chinese guide to strategy, now often cited for business and competitive tactics
ex: Before the merger talks, Jamal reread The Art of War for tips on negotiating.
The coach often quotes The Art of War, urging players to outthink opponents rather than overpower them.

cloze.s: “Know your enemy and know yourself,” the CEO said, quoting Sun Tzu's ___.

story: In the 1977 film Star Wars, Obi-Wan Kenobi uses the Force to tell imperial stormtroopers “These aren't the droids you're looking for,” and they obediently repeat it and let him pass.
def: a smooth bit of persuasion that gets someone to believe or do something without realizing it
ex: Priya pulled a Jedi mind trick on her kids, convincing them broccoli was “tiny trees for dinosaurs.”
The salesman's Jedi mind trick had me buying the extended warranty before I knew it.

cloze.s: Somehow Liam talked the bouncer into letting us in without tickets—a real ___.

story: In Ira Levin's 1972 novel The Stepford Wives, filmed in 1975, the women of a Connecticut suburb are secretly replaced by perfectly obedient robot look-alikes.
def: a woman who seems robotically submissive, perfectly groomed, and eager to please her husband
ex: The old ads showed a Stepford wife smiling blankly while vacuuming in pearls.
Maria refused to play the Stepford wife at her husband's company parties.

cloze.s: Her eerie, constant smile and flawless housekeeping made the neighbors whisper that she was a ___.

note: Mildly insulting; implies mindless conformity rather than genuine contentment.

story: Shakespeare's Richard III opens with Richard saying, “Now is the winter of our discontent / Made glorious summer by this sun of York,” meaning the unhappy time has ended with his family's rise.
def: a period of widespread hardship, frustration, and unhappiness
ex: Months of layoffs and frozen pay made that year the company's winter of our discontent.
Fans called the team's long losing streak the winter of our discontent.

cloze.s: With strikes, shortages, and endless rain, newspapers dubbed that season ___.

note: In the play, the line says the bad times are over; it is often quoted as if they are starting.

story: In Shakespeare's Macbeth, Lady Macbeth goads her hesitant husband into murdering King Duncan so he can take the crown, and she is later tormented by guilt.
def: a ruthlessly ambitious woman who pushes someone close to her to do wrong for power
ex: The drama's villain is a Lady Macbeth who urges her husband to sabotage his rival.
Biographers argue the queen was unfairly painted as a Lady Macbeth pulling the strings.

cloze.s: In the novel, the senator's scheming wife plays ___, pressuring him to betray his best friend for power.

story: In Shakespeare's Antony and Cleopatra, Cleopatra dismisses her past love for Julius Caesar as belonging to “my salad days, / When I was green in judgment.”
def: the carefree time of one's youth and inexperience, or a period when one was at one's peak
ex: In his salad days, Grandpa hitchhiked across the country with just a guitar.
The record label's salad days ended when streaming changed the music business.

cloze.s: Looking at old photos from college, Olga laughed about the reckless choices of her ___.

story: Sir John Falstaff appears in Shakespeare's Henry IV plays and The Merry Wives of Windsor as a fat, merry, boastful knight who loves drink and dodges danger.
def: boisterously jolly, boastful, and fond of food and drink
ex: Uncle Kofi has a Falstaffian laugh that fills the room at every family feast.
The actor brought a Falstaffian swagger to the role of the pirate captain.

cloze.s: With his huge appetite, booming jokes, and tall tales, the innkeeper was a truly ___ figure.

story: In Macbeth, after learning of his wife's death, Macbeth calls life “a tale / Told by an idiot, full of sound and fury, / Signifying nothing.”
def: loud, dramatic, and emotional but ultimately meaningless
ex: The press conference was full of sound and fury but offered no actual plan.
Their argument was full of sound and fury, yet by dinner neither remembered why it started.

cloze.s: The action movie was ___: endless explosions and no story worth remembering.

note: The fuller form ends “signifying nothing.”

story: In Macbeth, Lady Macbeth worries that her husband is “too full o' th' milk of human kindness” to seize the crown by murder.
def: natural compassion, warmth, and sympathy toward other people
ex: The nurse who stayed past her shift to comfort the family was full of the milk of human kindness.
Neighbors showed the milk of human kindness, bringing meals after the fire.

cloze.s: The landlord, utterly lacking ___, evicted the family in the middle of winter.

story: In Shakespeare's Julius Caesar, Mark Antony, grieving over Caesar's body, predicts that Caesar's spirit will “Cry ‘Havoc!’ and let slip the dogs of war.”
def: the violence, chaos, and destruction unleashed when armed conflict begins
ex: Diplomats worked for weeks to keep the dogs of war leashed.
Once the border clash began, the dogs of war were let loose across the region.

cloze.s: The general warned that a single rash decision could unleash the ___ for a generation.

story: In Shakespeare's The Winter's Tale, the character Antigonus leaves the stage under the famous stage direction “Exit, pursued by a bear,” and is later reported killed offstage.
def: a joking phrase for a sudden, hasty, or comically undignified departure
ex: “Exit, pursued by a bear,” Tomás joked as he raced out of the meeting before anyone could ask questions.
The director's abrupt resignation email read like a stage direction: exit, pursued by a bear.

cloze.s: When the waiter brought the enormous bill, my uncle mumbled an excuse and fled—___.

term: a plague on both your houses
story: In Romeo and Juliet, Mercutio, fatally wounded in a brawl between the feuding Montagues and Capulets, curses both families: “A plague o' both your houses!”
def: an expression of disgust with both sides in a dispute, blaming each equally
ex: Tired of the neighbors' endless fence fight, Hannah said, “A plague on both your houses.”
The editorial took a plague on both your houses view of the two feuding unions.

cloze.s: Fed up with her squabbling roommates, Yuki moved out with a final “___!”
cloze.a: A plague on both your houses

story: In Jonathan Swift's Gulliver's Travels (1726), Gulliver is shipwrecked on Lilliput, an island of people about six inches tall who are obsessed with petty quarrels.
def: extremely small; also petty or trivial in importance
ex: The Lilliputian apartment had a kitchen the size of a closet.
The council wasted hours on Lilliputian arguments about the color of park benches.

cloze.s: Next to the giant cruise ship, our little fishing boat looked ___.

story: Lothario is the charming seducer in Nicholas Rowe's 1703 play The Fair Penitent, who wins and then abandons a young woman; his name became a byword for a heartless seducer.
def: a man who charms and seduces women, then casually moves on
ex: The soap opera's resident Lothario has dated half the town.
Sofia's friends warned her that the smooth-talking surgeon was a notorious Lothario.

cloze.s: Charming at first, he turned out to be a ___ with three girlfriends who didn't know about one another.

story: Mrs. Malaprop, a character in Richard Brinsley Sheridan's 1775 comedy The Rivals, constantly uses the wrong words, as in “as headstrong as an allegory on the banks of the Nile”; her name comes from French mal à propos, “inappropriately.”
def: the mistaken use of a word that sounds like the right one, with a silly result
ex: Grandpa's malapropism—calling the rumor “a pigment of her imagination”—made everyone laugh.
The coach's malapropism about staying “pacifically” focused became a locker-room joke.

cloze.s: When Malik bragged about his “photogenic memory” instead of a photographic one, his sister teased him for the ___.

note: Not the same as a spoonerism, which swaps sounds between words.

story: The names first appeared in an 18th-century epigram by John Byrom mocking a rivalry between the composers Handel and Bononcini; Lewis Carroll made them famous as near-identical twins in Through the Looking-Glass (1871).
def: two people or things that are practically indistinguishable despite claiming to differ
ex: The two phone plans were Tweedledum and Tweedledee—same price, same data, different logos.
Critics called the rival sequels Tweedledum and Tweedledee, both recycling the same plot.

cloze.s: The two brands of bottled water were ___: same source, same taste, same price.

story: In George Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four, doublethink is the ability the ruling Party demands of citizens: to hold two contradictory beliefs at once and accept both.
def: simultaneously believing two contradictory ideas, usually through propaganda or self-deception
ex: It takes doublethink to praise healthy eating while stocking candy in every school hallway.
The memo's doublethink described the pay cuts as a “compensation enhancement.”

cloze.s: Insisting the store was both losing money and doing great required a kind of ___ from the manager.

story: Thomas Hobson (c. 1544–1631) rented out horses in Cambridge, England, and made each customer take the horse nearest the stable door or none at all.
def: an apparent selection in which only one option is actually offered: take it or leave it
ex: With only one airline serving the island, travelers face a Hobson's choice.
Accept the transfer or lose your job—that's a Hobson's choice, not a real option.

cloze.s: The cafeteria offered one meal or nothing, a ___ that left Jamal hungry.

note: Not the same as a dilemma, which offers two or more bad options.

story: English physician Thomas Bowdler published The Family Shakespeare in the early 1800s, cutting words and passages he considered unsuitable for reading aloud to a family.
def: to remove material considered improper from a text, often weakening it
ex: The TV network bowdlerized the movie so heavily that the plot no longer made sense.
Students protested when the school bowdlerized classic novels for its reading list.

cloze.s: The publisher ___ the memoir, cutting every swear word and spicy scene.

story: Reverend William Archibald Spooner (1844–1930), an Oxford college head, was famous for accidentally swapping the first sounds of words; many examples credited to him were probably invented by others.
def: a slip of the tongue in which the first sounds of two words are swapped
ex: Saying “a blushing crow” instead of “a crushing blow” is a classic spoonerism.
Nervous at the podium, Wei produced a spoonerism, saying “tons of soil” when he meant “sons of toil.”

cloze.s: “You have hissed all my mystery lectures” is a famous ___ attributed to an Oxford professor.

note: Different from a malapropism, which substitutes a wrong but similar-sounding word.

story: English economist Thomas Robert Malthus argued in An Essay on the Principle of Population (1798) that population tends to grow faster than the food supply, leading to famine and misery.
def: relating to the gloomy view that population growth will outrun resources and cause disaster
ex: Malthusian fears of mass famine faded as farming technology boosted crop yields.
The documentary took a Malthusian view of water shortages in fast-growing cities.

cloze.s: The professor predicted that rising population would soon exhaust the planet's food, a classic ___ warning.

story: Grigory Potemkin, an adviser to Russia's Catherine the Great, was said to have built fake village fronts along her 1787 tour of Crimea to impress her; historians believe the story is largely exaggerated.
def: an impressive false front built to hide a poor or embarrassing reality
ex: The freshly painted model classroom was a Potemkin village for the visiting inspectors.
Analysts suspected the firm's glossy headquarters was a Potemkin village hiding mounting debt.

cloze.s: The landlord renovated only the lobby before the tour, a ___ hiding broken heaters upstairs.

story: The Byzantine Empire, the eastern Roman Empire ruled from Constantinople until 1453, gained a reputation in the West, partly exaggerated, for elaborate bureaucracy and court intrigue.
def: excessively complicated and hard to navigate, often involving secretive scheming
ex: The university's Byzantine registration system requires six signatures for one class.
Office politics at the firm were Byzantine, with alliances shifting every week.

cloze.s: The tax rules were so ___ that even the accountant needed a flowchart to follow them.

note: Often written lowercase (byzantine).

story: Laconia was the region of ancient Greece ruled by Sparta, whose people were famous for terse speech; according to ancient writers, when Philip II of Macedon threatened what he would do if he invaded, the Spartans replied simply, “If.”
def: using very few words; brief and to the point in speech
ex: The laconic rancher answered every question with “Yep” or “Nope.”
Her laconic text—just “Fine.”—told Diego she was still upset.

cloze.s: Known for his ___ style, the coach summed up the painful loss in two words: “We lost.”

story: On October 4, 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite; the shock spurred the United States to pour money into science education and to create NASA in 1958.
def: a jolting event that reveals a rival has pulled ahead and spurs a push to catch up
ex: Some called a rival country's breakthrough in AI a Sputnik moment for American tech.
The dismal math scores were a Sputnik moment for the school district.

cloze.s: When a foreign team won the robotics contest by a mile, engineers called it a ___ that demanded new funding.

story: Mary Mallon (1869–1938), an Irish-born cook in the New York area, was a healthy carrier of typhoid fever who infected many people she cooked for; health officials isolated her for much of her later life.
def: a person who spreads disease or some harmful influence, often without realizing it
ex: Coughing through the office all week, Liam was the Typhoid Mary of flu season.
The intern became the Typhoid Mary of bad habits, spreading shortcuts to every new hire.

cloze.s: The daycare traced the stomach bug to one sick child, a tiny ___ who had shared toys with everyone.

story: In studies at Western Electric's Hawthorne Works near Chicago in the 1920s and 1930s, workers' productivity seemed to rise whenever conditions changed, perhaps because they knew they were being studied; later reanalyses questioned the findings.
def: the tendency of people to change their behavior because they know they are being observed
ex: Hand-washing rates jumped while the inspectors were watching—a clear Hawthorne effect.
Researchers worried that the Hawthorne effect would inflate the results of their diet study.

cloze.s: The cashiers were extra polite only during the week managers were watching, a textbook ___.

story: British physician Richard Asher named the disorder in 1951 after Baron Münchhausen, an 18th-century German nobleman whose name was attached to a popular book of wildly exaggerated tall tales.
def: a mental disorder in which a person repeatedly fakes or causes illness to get medical attention
ex: Doctors suspected Munchausen syndrome after the patient visited eleven hospitals with invented symptoms.
The documentary explored how Munchausen syndrome can fool even experienced physicians.

cloze.s: The man faked heart attacks at emergency rooms across three states, a pattern typical of ___.

note: Now formally called factitious disorder; doing it to another person is factitious disorder imposed on another.

story: British historian C. Northcote Parkinson opened a humorous 1955 essay in The Economist with the line “Work expands so as to fill the time available for its completion.”
def: the observation that work stretches to fill however much time is allowed for it
ex: Given a month to write a two-page report, Kwame proved Parkinson's law by finishing the night before.
Some managers set tight deadlines on purpose to fight Parkinson's law.

cloze.s: The team had a week for a one-day task and somehow needed the whole week—___ in action.

note: Unrelated to Parkinson's disease, which is named after the physician James Parkinson.

story: In their 1969 book The Peter Principle, Laurence J. Peter and Raymond Hull argued that in a hierarchy, employees keep getting promoted until they reach a job they cannot do well.
def: the idea that people get promoted until they land in a role beyond their competence
ex: The brilliant engineer became a hopeless manager, a textbook case of the Peter principle.
To avoid the Peter principle, the hospital lets great nurses earn raises without moving into administration.

cloze.s: The star salesman was promoted to director and floundered at once—the ___ at work.

story: Canadian media theorist Marshall McLuhan introduced the phrase in his 1964 book Understanding Media, arguing that each technology, such as television, changes society through its form, not just its content.
def: the idea that the way information is delivered shapes its effect as much as the content does
ex: A handwritten thank-you note shows that the medium is the message.
Teens texting instead of calling proves the medium is the message, the sociologist argued.

cloze.s: The CEO announced the layoffs by text, and staff felt the cold delivery said it all; ___.

story: Around AD 100, the Roman satirist Juvenal complained that the people, who once handed out power and armies, now longed for only two things: “bread and circuses,” meaning free grain and public games.
def: food and entertainment provided to keep the public distracted and content rather than engaged
ex: Critics called the free concerts bread and circuses meant to distract from rising taxes.
The endless streaming binge felt like bread and circuses while real problems piled up.

cloze.s: The town threw festivals with free food every weekend, offering ___ so people wouldn't ask about the missing budget.

note: From the Latin panem et circenses.
